Modern · The Seoul Table

Ssam with Ssamjang

A fresh, generous ssam table, built around the flavor of the fermented pastes.

Korean · Easy · Serves 4 (the modern ssam spread)

Jump to recipe ↓

Behind the dish

Lane: modern — the ssam bar, built around the pastes. The ssam table's grammar (the leaf, the sauce, the meat, the fold) belongs to the grill site's tradition (#F01 there); this record is the modern spread — a gochujang-spiked ssamjang, quick seared fillings, and a build-your-own board that turns a weeknight into a ssam bar. The paste runs the whole board: the ssamjang's heat, a cho-gochujang dip for the vegetables, and a lacquered pan-seared pork that takes ten minutes. Heat dial: 3, dropping to 2 if the table skews mild.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Both sauces whisked first — the ssamjang worked to one color (the #SA01 law), the cho-gochujang whisked to a spooning looseness (the gochujang-lane's acid partnership).
  • The leaves dried completely; the fillings sliced; the board assembled before the pan — searing runs eight minutes and the table builds itself around the hot pork.

Let’s make it.

  1. 01
    The pork seared in batches at high heat, pulled to the board, and scissored into bite pieces. Checkpoint — browned edges, juicy centers, and the pan's fond left behind — deglaze it with a spoon of water and scrape the drippings into the ssamjang bowl (the old restaurant move: the sauce drinks the meat's flavor).
  2. 02
    The board: sauces at center, pork warm beside, leaves, rice, garlic, and chili in their quadrants. Checkpoint — every seat reaches all five — leaf, both sauces, pork, rice — without a pass. The board's geometry is the recipe's architecture.
  3. 03
    The build, the tradition's own sequence: leaf, a swipe of ssamjang (or the cho-gochujang for the sweet-heat fork), a piece of hot pork, a garlic coin, a pinch of rice, fold, one bite. Checkpoint — the eating test between the two sauces' bites: the ssamjang's fermented depth against the cho-gochujang's bright-sweet-heat — the same pork, two different sauces, two different ssams. That comparison is the board's whole evening. Chef’s Note — the ssam bar is the modern ssam's honest form: the tradition's fold-the-meal grammar, lifted out of the grill-theater and set on a weeknight table with fast fillings. The rule that survives every adaptation is the fold's — one bite, everything in it, the leaf closed without tearing. A ssam that needs two bites was built by greed; the leaf is the portion's limit, and the kitchen sends more leaves.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Ssamjang flatMissing the fond or the honeyDeglaze into it; both are load-bearing
Cho-gochujang too thick to swipeUnder-loosenedWater by the splash; vinegar by the taste
Leaves tearing at the foldWet leaves or overfillingBone-dry; the fold is one bite's worth
Board assembled coldPan came before the boardBoard first, always — the sear is the last act

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Both sauces keep a week refrigerated and improve; the board is a night's event. Seared pork keeps 3 days for the lunchbox ssam.
  • Variations: the #SF11-style seared tofu for the plant table; bulgogi slices (#M01's build) for the fuller board; a bowl of the kimchi (#2) as the board's third sauce in solid form.
